title: Early Behavioral Consequences and Neuroendocrine Adaptations to Intermittent Social Defeat During Adolescence: Differential Effects of Orexin, Galanin and Neuropeptide Y
content: Repeated psychosocial stress during adolescence can produce behavioural and neurobiological consequences that extend beyond the period of stress exposure, yet the endogenous systems regulating these responses remain incompletely understood. Orexinergic, galaninergic and neuropeptide Y (NPY) signalling are involved in stress regulation, but their contribution when repeatedly engaged during adverse social experiences has not been directly compared. Here, we investigated how pharmacological modulation of these three stress-responsive systems during intermittent social defeat in late-adolescent male mice influenced early behavioural outcomes and persistent molecular alterations. Mice received the selective orexin-2 receptor agonist YNT-185 (20 mg/kg), the galanin receptor agonist Galnon (10 mg/kg), NPY (0.06 mg/kg), or vehicle before each of four social defeat or control-exploration sessions. Behaviour was assessed 24–48 h after the final session, whereas hippocampal glucocorticoid receptor (GR) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and prefrontal cortical tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) were quantified five weeks later. Intermittent social defeat reduced open-arm exploration, social interaction, grooming and tail-suspension immobility, demonstrating alterations across anxiety-related, social, depression-related and stress-coping domains. Five weeks later, previously defeated mice exhibited reduced hippocampal GR and BDNF and reduced prefrontal TNF-α and IL-1β, revealing persistent alterations across neuroendocrine, neuroplasticity-related and neuroimmune markers. Pharmacological modulation also affected behavioural and molecular measures in non-defeated animals, demonstrating that these systems regulate the examined processes independently of stress exposure. During social defeat, Galnon and YNT-185 selectively attenuated the deficit in social interaction, whereas NPY did not produce a comparable effect; none of the three manipulations broadly normalized the behavioural or persistent molecular profile associated with defeat. Individual variation in the early behavioural outcomes was not significantly correlated with the molecular markers measured five weeks later, supporting their interpretation as temporally distinct consequences rather than direct behavioural–molecular correlates. Together, these findings show that modulation of galaninergic, orexinergic and NPY signalling during repeated adolescent social experiences produces distinct context-dependent effects and identify persistent molecular consequences of intermittent social defeat that remain detectable weeks after stress cessation.
